data.title: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
data.description: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices. Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years. Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year. “I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’” Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines. U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period. This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars — including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers — for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago. Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa — which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate -- and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February. But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales. Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year. “People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.” The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales. “We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

data.title: U.S. airlines favor higher fares over fuller planes as fuel costs squeeze profits
data.description: U.S. airlines are increasingly willing to fly with empty seats rather than slash fares simply to fill ​them, betting that disciplined pricing and flight schedules will help protect profits at a time of soaring fuel costs. The strategy has delivered substantial revenue gains as demand has ‌held up despite sharp fare increases. Yet profits have still been squeezed as jet fuel prices surged roughly 90% since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, forcing several major carriers to cut earnings forecasts. Executives at Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group have emphasized protecting margins over boosting passenger volumes. Their resolve faces a test in 2027. Industry schedules point to more flying capacity, potentially intensifying competition for passengers even as fuel ​prices are expected to stay high and making this year’s substantial fare gains harder to repeat. “If fuel stays elevated, we have to continue to push yield up so that ​we can make a bit of money,” American Chief Financial Officer Devon May told Reuters on Thursday. Yield is the revenue airlines collect for each ⁠mile passengers fly. Six major U.S. airlines plan to grow domestic capacity 3.0% in the fourth quarter from a year earlier and 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027, a sharp acceleration from just ​0.2% growth in the third quarter, according to Airlines for America, citing Cirium data. U.S. air fares rose an average of nearly 23% year-on-year in the seven months through September, far outpacing the 3.6% average ​increase in overall consumer prices, according to Labor Department data. Airlines are still seeking increases. JetBlue Airways initiated a $10 one-way increase in domestic published fares on Wednesday, JP Morgan said, following a similar United-led increase the previous week that Southwest subsequently matched. United said it had nothing further to add, while Southwest said it does not publicly discuss pricing. JetBlue did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A different approach Airlines have long balanced fares against how full their ​planes are. But elevated fuel costs have made executives more willing to sacrifice occupancy and avoid discounts. United’s commercial chief Andrew Nocella offered an example during Wednesday’s earnings call. Its leisure load factor, ​a measure of how many available seats are occupied, fell 1.3 percentage points in the third quarter. Nocella acknowledged that the decline showed “a small amount of elasticity given higher ticket prices,” but called it “a trade we would make ‌every day.” American ⁠Airlines planes flew less full in the third quarter even as passenger yields jumped more than 18%. Finance chief May told Reuters the trade was deliberate. Delta has also been “managing the business for margins,” CEO Ed Bastian said. Across Delta, United, American, Southwest and Alaska, passenger revenue rose nearly $8.8 billion, or 18%, in the third quarter from a year earlier, while passenger traffic increased less than 1%. The divergence shows how much revenue growth now depends on earning more from each passenger rather than carrying more of them. Premium products and changes in passenger mix have also contributed to the gains. The Transportation Security Administration ​screened 2.9% fewer people at U.S. airports in ​the quarter than a year earlier, raising questions ⁠about whether higher fares are beginning to discourage travel. Limited capacity growth and the shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines have also weighed on traffic. Airline executives insisted that demand remains resilient. “Those higher fares are not causing an erosion of volumes,” Southwest CEO Bob Jordan told analysts, after the airline ​reported a nearly 22% increase in average passenger fares in the first nine months of this year. The 2027 test But record revenues have not been ​enough to shield profits from ⁠soaring fuel costs. Gulf Coast spot jet fuel prices have risen from $2.43 a gallon before the war began in February to $4.63 on October 20, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data. Delta and Southwest have cut their annual earnings forecasts, while American expects a full-year loss despite sharply higher passenger revenue. Airlines are now scrutinizing expansion plans. American intends to slow growth considerably next year, with May saying the carrier was reassessing whether additional flights ⁠would generate enough ​revenue to cover their operating costs. Southwest has pledged not to pursue growth at the expense of profitability, while United ​executives have cautioned that airlines’ published 2027 capacity plans may not materialize. Such restraint could help maintain higher fares. But flying less can raise operating costs per seat, while pushing prices higher risks discouraging travelers who have already absorbed steep increases. But airline ​executives say a disciplined approach on capacity can allow the industry to hold on to pricing gains. “We think these yield gains are very sustainable,” May said.

data.title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
data.description: Etsy announced new restrictions Thursday on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of its sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud. Among the new stipulations: Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.Bot-generated listings are banned. AI-generated art can still be sold on the platform as long as merchants “Play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process,” Etsy said in a note to sellers. “Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post. “Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it. We know we have work to do to uphold this standard on Etsy.” Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of whom are women who run one-person businesses out of their homes, according to an annual company report. That distinguishes it from other major e-commerce platforms like Amazon and eBay, though it commands a fraction of those platforms’ revenues. As of 2024, Etsy hosted $10.9 billion-worth of goods’ sales, compared with about $75 billion for eBay and more than $700 billion for Amazon. Some buyers responded positively to Etsy’s announcement. “I can’t explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realize it’s fully AI-generated, doesn’t make sense, and definitely doesn’t match what the finished product should be,” creator Kara Lynne said on X. The dawn of advanced AI has led to an explosion in AI-generated sales content — and a growing backlash from consumers against what they see as AI slop. A recent social media trend among cafes and restaurants saw owners pledging not to use AI after egregious examples of AI-generated food images in the wild were shared on social media. Major platforms are responding to the growing discontent. Many, including Facebook and Instagram, now work to append labels to images or videos created via AI. Others, like LinkedIn, have added buttons allowing users to report AI-generated content. Snap has banned wholly AI-generated content from its recommendation algorithm, while Spotify recently announced it had removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its platform. Ossman said Etsy would add a function similar to LinkedIn’s that makes it easier for users to report listings that include misleading AI imagery. He also said Etsy would be using technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months. “We’re actively working to address the questions AI raises for our marketplace,” Ossman said in the post. “This work is hard, and we don’t have every answer today. But I believe this is an important moment for Etsy, and that these initial steps are putting us on the right path.”

data.title: Trump promised $2 gas and cheaper groceries. Here’s what voters got instead.
data.description: When voters headed to the polls nearly two years ago, Donald Trump promised them cheaper groceries, gas below $2 a gallon and a wave of new manufacturing jobs. They elected him president — and got the opposite.

data.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer ask guests to clean dishes or make beds
data.description: Airbnb hosts can only set “reasonable” housecleaning duties for guests, according to new guidelines rolled out by the tech giant, with tasks such as dishwashing and bed stripping now the sole responsibility of homeowners. While Airbnb bookings have always included a cleaning fee, there hadn’t been universal policies on what hosts can ask their renters to complete. But now, starting with rentals on Nov. 20, Airbnb will limit these guest responsibilities in order to “set clear expectations” for hosts whose house rules must be “reasonable and comply with” these new requirements. Hosts cannot ask “guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes,” Airbnb said. The new guidelines come after years of customer complaints, travel industry expert Clint Henderson told NBC News. “So this is pretty major for consumers,” said Henderson, managing editor and spokesperson for travel industry website The Points Guy. “The complaints have been really ramping up lately with owners asking guests to do the most ridiculous things, like stripping beds, washing dishes, doing all the laundry and taking the trash out,” Henderson said. “It’s just gotten really out of hand,” he said. “And from a consumer’s perspective, it’s like, ‘Why am I going to stay at Airbnb when I have to do chores?’” While Airbnb host Gabriel Valk, in Greenville, South Carolina, believes small tasks like dishwashing and bed stripping should be “common courtesy” performed by guests, he understands why Airbnb would institute these more clear guidelines. “But I do understand the pushback,” Valk said, citing the service fees that are supposed to cover cleaning costs. “OK, you guys are paying, whatever, $100 for the cleaning. ‘We shouldn’t have to do anything,’” he imagined the guests saying. “So totally makes sense to me.” Airbnb had to give guests a break or risk consumers flocking back to traditional hotels, according to Henderson. “Why (stay at an Airbnb) when I can stay at a hotel and not have to do all that busy work?” he said. “And these days, Airbnb is as expensive, with all the fees and everything, as a hotel is. So I think Airbnb has lost some of its competitive edge over the years.”

data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by more than 40% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of more than $4 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In six states — Alaska, California, Hawaii, Oregon, Nevada and Washington — average gas prices are at least $5 per gallon. Georgia, Ohio and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $70 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, were approaching pre-war levels, and are now surging again as turmoil in the Middle East continues. Since mid-May, the average national gas price has declined by around 20 cents. The average price is still up more than a dollar per gallon since the start of the war.

data.title: How Victoria’s Secret CEO Hillary Super is reconnecting a storied brand with its customers
data.description: When Hillary Super became the CEO of Victoria’s Secret & Co. in 2024, she took on a difficult task: reconnecting the iconic lingerie company with a customer base it had been losing gradually for a decade.

data.title: How safe are roller coasters? What riders should know
data.description: After a roller-coaster death this week in Georgia, amusement parkgoers are asking how thrill rides are regulated across the country in the absence of nationwide safety standards.

data.title: Americans’ eating habits are changing. For Chick-fil-A, adapting to them is a tall order
data.description: Chick-fil-A is a company that cherishes its past. The third-largest restaurant chain in America hasn’t changed the recipe for its signature chicken sandwich since it debuted in 1967. From the beginning, Chick-fil-A has been a private, family-owned business and it intends to stay that way.

data.title: Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
data.description: Social Security recipients will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment next year of 3.6%, one of the largest increases this decade. But advocates say it’s still unlikely to go far enough for many struggling seniors. The increase is the largest since 2022, and will amount to an average monthly increase of about $70, according to the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans. Elevated inflation continues to bedevil the U.S. economy, with rising energy and gas prices sparked by wars in Iran and Ukraine as the primary culprits. Yet even without the added cost of gas, so-called core inflation — which excludes volatile energy and food prices — has remained stuck at about 2.5%, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. For senior citizens, who are the majority of Social Security retirement benefit recipients, next year’s increase will be welcome, but it will still come up short given rising costs, said Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director. “Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Benton said. “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.” The league found in a survey that 89% of older Americans thought the cost-of-living adjustment that kicked in this year, 2.8%, was inadequate given rising costs in the economy. About 44% of seniors draw all their income from Social Security, the survey found. The annual adjustment is typically calculated using inflation data from July, August and September. But it uses an obscure inflation index that advocates say doesn’t accurately reflect seniors’ spending priorities, which include more medical and prescription drug costs, as well as a greater likelihood that they will pay rent and generally higher home energy costs. Those categories have historically outpaced headline inflation, though the rate of medical-cost increases has slowed recently. One reform proposal would index the annual adjustment to more precisely reflect seniors’ needs — but Benton said it is unlikely to be adopted until all of Social Security is overhauled. “They need Social Security benefits to cover the cost of living, and it’s just not happening,” she said.
